title: Quartiles and interquartile range
keyIdea: Put the data in order first. The median cuts the ordered list in half. The lower quartile (Q1) is the median of the lower half and the upper quartile (Q3) is the median of the upper half; with an odd number of values, leave the median out of both halves. For n values, Q1 is the (n + 1)/4 th value and Q3 the 3(n + 1)/4 th. The interquartile range is IQR = Q3 − Q1: the spread of the middle half of the data. Unlike the range (largest − smallest), the IQR ignores the extreme ends, so one outlier barely changes it. Compare groups with the median for a typical value and the IQR for consistency.
familyTip: Write down how many minutes each person at home spent on a phone or reading yesterday, or use a sports team’s scores. Put them in order together, find the median, then Q1 and Q3. Ask: who is typical, and how spread out is the middle half?

visual.caption: Range or IQR: which one does each fact describe? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: order the data, tap the median and quartiles, stretch a box from Q1 to Q3, drag an outlier, and compare two players.

kid: Quartiles split data into four equal parts. First, put the values in order. The middle value is the median. It splits the data into a lower half and an upper half.
The lower quartile, Q1, is the middle of the lower half. The upper quartile, Q3, is the middle of the upper half. If there is an odd number of values, leave the median out of both halves.
The interquartile range is Q3 minus Q1. It tells you how spread out the middle half of the data is. A small IQR means the values are close together, so the data are consistent.

The range is largest minus smallest, so one very big or very small value changes it a lot. The IQR ignores the ends, so it hardly changes. That makes the IQR a fairer measure of spread when there are outliers.
adult: Ages 13 to 15. In England this is the KS3 and GCSE statistics content: interpret, analyse and compare distributions through measures of central tendency (median) and spread (range, quartiles and interquartile range), leading to box plots and cumulative frequency. In the US it matches Common Core 6.SP.B.5c and 7.SP.B.3–4 (IQR as a measure of variability) and S-ID.A.2.

Method used here: order the n values; the median is the (n + 1)/2 th value; Q1 is the median of the values below the median and Q3 of those above it, which for small sets matches the GCSE (n + 1)/4 th and 3(n + 1)/4 th positions. The lab uses 7 and 11 values, where these methods agree exactly. Other methods (including the median in each half, or calculators’ interpolation) can give slightly different quartiles for other n, so check which method an exam board or calculator uses.

IQR = Q3 − Q1 measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data. Because it ignores the lowest and highest quarters, it is resistant to outliers, while the range is not. To compare distributions, quote a measure of average (median) and a measure of spread (IQR) in context: a smaller IQR means more consistent values.

Common mistakes: finding quartiles from unsorted data; taking Q1 as a quarter of the way along the range (smallest + range ÷ 4) instead of a quarter of the way through the ordered list; counting the median in a half and so landing one place off; giving the range when asked for the IQR; and saying a bigger IQR is better or more consistent.

practice.prompt: Data in order: 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 12. What is the lower quartile?
practice.hint: Q1 is the middle of the lower half: the values below the median.
practice.explain: The median is 7, the 4th value. The lower half is 2, 4, 5, and its middle is 4, so Q1 = 4.

practice.prompt: The lower quartile of a data set is {a} and the upper quartile is {b}. What is the interquartile range?
A data set has {n} values in order. Which position is the median? (Give the value number.)
practice.hint: The median is the (n + 1)/2 th value.
practice.explain: ({n} + 1) ÷ 2 = {=(n+1)/2}, so the median is value number {=(n+1)/2} in the ordered list.

practice.hint: Put the values in order before you look for the middle.
practice.explain: In order: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21. The middle (4th) value is 12. The 4th value of the unsorted list is 12 by luck here, but always sort first.

practice.prompt: A class’s quiz marks have an IQR of 6. One pupil scores 0. What happens?
choices: The range grows, but the IQR barely changes
practice.hint: The IQR only uses the middle half of the data.
practice.explain: A score of 0 stretches the range because it is a new smallest value. Q1 and Q3 move little or not at all, so the IQR barely changes.

pool.prompt: What does the interquartile range measure?
choices: the spread of the middle half of the data
the difference between largest and smallest
pool.hint: Think about which two values the IQR uses.
pool.explain: IQR = Q3 − Q1, so it measures how spread out the middle half is. The middle value is the median, and largest − smallest is the range.

pool.prompt: Data: 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, 16, 20. What is the upper quartile?
pool.hint: With 11 values, the upper half is the 5 values above the median.
pool.explain: The median is 9, the 6th value. The upper half is 11, 13, 14, 16, 20, and its middle is 14, so Q3 = 14.

pool.prompt: Q1 is {a} and Q3 is {b}. What is the IQR?
pool.hint: Subtract the lower quartile from the upper quartile.

pool.prompt: An ordered data set has {n} values. Q1 is which value number in the list?
pool.explain: ({n} + 1) ÷ 4 = {=(n+1)/4}, so Q1 is value number {=(n+1)/4} in the ordered list.

pool.prompt: Data: 4, 8, 10, 12, 30. Why is the IQR better than the range for describing spread here?
choices: 30 is an outlier, and the IQR ignores the extreme ends
pool.hint: Which value looks far away from the rest?
pool.explain: 30 is far from the others, so the range (26) is stretched. The IQR uses only the middle half, so it is not pulled by one extreme value.

pool.prompt: Team A: median 20, IQR 3. Team B: median 20, IQR 11. Which statement is right?
choices: Team A’s scores are more consistent
Team B’s scores are more consistent
pool.hint: Same median, so compare the spread.
pool.explain: The medians match, so typical scores are the same. Team A’s smaller IQR means its middle scores are closer together: more consistent.

pool.prompt: Jo finds Q1 for 2, 5, 6, 9, 20, 22, 26 as 2 + (26 − 2) ÷ 4 = 8. What went wrong?
choices: Q1 is a position in the ordered list, not a quarter of the range
She forgot to order the data
pool.hint: Quartiles count values, not distance along the number line.
pool.explain: Q1 is the middle of the lower half: 2, 5, 6, so Q1 = 5. Adding a quarter of the range finds a point on the number line, not a quartile.

pool.hint: Sort first, then find Q1 and Q3.
pool.explain: In order: 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11. Q1 = 4 and Q3 = 9, so IQR = 9 − 4 = 5. 9 is the range (11 − 2) and 3 is not a quartile gap.
